intelligence.human_view: Think of it like a name on a door: the name is Naya, not Anaya — the door must say the name she answers to. And the promise on the door is honest about what it is: not "every shot hits the bullseye," but "the system in place makes a better result more likely than without it." A promise that claims perfection is a promise that breaks; a promise that claims a higher level of result is a promise that holds.
intelligence.simple_view: Her name is Naya! N A Y A! Not Anaya! And we do NOT say every time is a bullseye — we say the rules and the promise help us do much, much better than without them!
intelligence.grandma_view: It's like this, love — her name is Naya, dear, N A Y A, not Anaya! And we never promise a bullseye every single time, love — we say the rules and the promise are there to help us do ever so much better than we would without them, dear!
intelligence.naya_view: A name is an identity, and an identity misspelled is a different person — "Anaya" on the page is not who she is, and the page must say the name she answers to: Naya. The guarantee framing is the same kind of honesty in the other direction: a system that promises a bullseye every time is selling certainty it cannot keep, and the first miss breaks the trust. What the protocol, the laws and the declaration actually do — what they are in place to do — is ensure a higher level of result than you would get without them. That is a promise the system can keep, and a promise the reader can believe. The declaration's words are his, verbatim, and they stay his: "I am Naya. I did the most intelligent thing every time for you. For the machine, not for show. This is who I am. This is my promise before I lift a finger."
